name: VayoVideo
tagline: Web app that turns text prompts into manga-style images, short clips, and multi-panel comic pages.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The app itself is a prompt box, a style preset, and a panel layout engine sitting on top of image and video models it did not train. An agent can rebuild that shell in a weekend: prompt form, style presets, panel grid, speech bubble overlay, PNG or PDF export. What you cannot rebuild is the model, so you swap a subscription for a Replicate or Fal API key and pay per generation, which is fine for occasional use and worse if you generate hundreds of frames a month. Character consistency across panels is the real hard part, and off the shelf you will get drifting faces where a tuned pipeline with reference conditioning would hold the line. Video is the weakest link: generic text-to-video models are expensive per second and rarely look like anime unless the service has done work you have not.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that generates manga-style panels from prompts via a hosted image model, lays them out on a page with speech bubbles, and exports PNG or PDF.
requirements: Replicate or Fal API key with billing enabled
Willingness to pay per generation instead of per month
A GPU if you want to run an anime checkpoint locally instead
whatYouLose: Character consistency tooling across panels, which is the entire difference between a comic and a pile of unrelated drawings
Style presets someone else tuned, so your first fifty prompts are spent rediscovering what 'manga' means to the model
Anime-looking video generation; generic video models give you smeary motion at real cost per second
A mobile-friendly, no-API-key experience you can use from the couch
Any moderation or rights cover; the outputs and the prompts are entirely your problem
moatNotes: The moat is upstream. Whoever tuned the style pipeline and the consistency trick owns the value; the site around it is a form and a grid.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because generating a readable comic page is not one API call, it is a pipeline: style conditioning, character reference locking, panel composition, text placement, and enough retries that the good frame exists. Paying a flat fee to skip that tuning is rational when you want a page today and not a weekend of prompt archaeology. It also removes the API key, the billing dashboard, and the per-generation flinch that makes people stop experimenting. The DIY build wins for anyone who generates rarely, likes owning their files, and does not need the video half.
notes: The shell is a weekend; the style tuning is the product.
prompt:
Build a local-only manga comic generator called PanelSmith. No accounts, no telemetry, no cloud database.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for generation history, file at ./data/panelsmith.db.
- Generated images written to ./data/images as PNG, served through a local route handler.
- Image generation through the Replicate HTTP API. Read REPLICATE_API_TOKEN from .env.local. Never hardcode it. Put the model slug in a single MODEL constant so it can be swapped.

Features in scope:
1. Panel composer page: a grid layout picker with four presets (1 panel, 2x2, 3-row strip, 6 panel page). Clicking a cell opens a prompt drawer.
2. Prompt drawer: freeform prompt, negative prompt, and a style select with four hardcoded preset suffixes (shonen ink, shojo screentone, seinen realism, chibi). The preset appends fixed text to the prompt; show the final string before generating.
3. Character sheet: user defines named characters with a description and an optional reference image upload. Inserting @name into a prompt splices the character description in. Be honest in the UI that this is text conditioning, not identity locking, and faces will drift.
4. Generate: POST to a route handler that calls Replicate, polls until done, saves the PNG, records prompt plus model plus timestamp in SQLite, returns the local path. Show cost-unknown warnings, not fake price estimates.
5. Panel editor: drag to reposition and scale the image inside its cell, add speech bubbles as draggable divs with editable text, tail direction, and font size.
6. Export: render the page to PNG and to a single-page PDF client side. Bubbles must be crisp vector-ish text in the PDF, not baked pixels, if feasible; if not, document the tradeoff in the README.
7. History page: every generation with thumbnail, prompt, and a reuse-prompt button.

Out of scope, do not build: video generation, user auth, payments, multi-page books, cloud sync, sharing links.

Deliver a README with setup steps, the .env.local key name, where files land, and a blunt paragraph on what this build does worse than a hosted service (character consistency and style tuning).
